newsitem.title: UK: Old crop Europe wheat fades as more farmers sell.
newsitem.headline: Old crop Europe wheat fades as more farmers sell.

text.p: Increased farmer selling hit old crop wheat prices this week, while the new crop was helped by rain.
French farmers selling ahead of the arrival of the new crop drove old-crop wheat prices sharply lower this week but volumes remained limited, dealers said.
Meanwhile new-crop wheat prices eased over last week on improved prospects for the 1997 harvest following recent rainfall.
Barley prices eased earlier in sympathy with wheat but were helped on Friday by news the European Union cleared the export of 89,200 tonnes of barley at its weekly auction.
Sidelined buyers and sellers kept maize prices steady.
Rain since the last week of April has eased concerns over France's grain crop but this month's rainfall will be crucial, national grain office ONIC said this week.
Despite nearly four months of drought soft wheat producton in the main production basins of northern France remain unscathed, it said.

But the rain came too late to contain damage to winter grain in the far south, where yields may fall by 20 to 30 percent, ONIC said. However the region is not a major grain producer making up less than 10 percent of total area sown in France.

Despite the rain, water shortages persist. The environment ministry has said that it will maintain water restrictions taken in 27 departments or provinces to cope with low supplies as the drought situation remained "worrying".
News Saudi Arabia had launched an import tender to purchase 700,000 tonnes of feed barley from the world market for July delivery had no immediate impact on prices, dealers said.
Countries set to compete for the contract include Canada, Australia, the United States and the European Union.
Maize prices were steady as low prices drove sellers away. Prices fell sharply last week on improved crop conditions and prospects of prefential imports of non-EU maize to Spain and Portugal.
In the UK, the LIFFE future was largely the creature of a volatile sterling, spending much of the week moving in a close inverse relationship to the currency.
Physical activity tended to be overshadowed by volatile futures. Traders said there was increased farmer selling. "We can't sell it fast enough," one said.

He expressed concern over the UK's ability to dispose of its remaining old crop grain surplus in May and June, the final two months of the crop year. Although there have been ships loading, notably for Tunisia, "we need the big boats," he said. "We have three-quarters of a million tonnes still to move. In May and June that's going to be difficult to do."
The Home Grown Cereals Authority put the surplus remaining for the final two months at 6-700,000 tonnes, and warned over the possibility of a large wheat carryover into 1997-98.

The sentiment was not universal. Another trader felt the outlook was positive, with 250,000 to 275,000 likely to be shipped in May and June "quite reasonable". Another put the likely surplus at around 50,000 to 100,000 tonnes.
With scattered showers for much of the week, the market does appear to have got the weather out of its system, for the time being at least, traders said.
In Germany, trading in old crop was subdued on Friday morning ahead of the long weekend holiday.
New crop wheat was largely at parity with the old crop, both in domestic and export markets, but buyers were not emerging, brokers said.

Brokers said German wheat prices were set to ease along with other European origins over the next few weeks but fears of possible heatwaves in western and southern Europe were underpinning wheat and maize levels.
Barley sellers were still offering what brokers consider a cheap 247.50-255 marks a tonne range on the new crop.
The latest EU approval for the export of German intervention barley was supportive for prices, but barley sellers were keen to free storage space for wheat, brokers said.
Another problem for barley, which is prevalent in pig feed rations, remains the Dutch swine fever outbreak, which has dampened deamnd.
Feed rye was hard to place but there was some demand for bread rye.
German intervention stores to date have absorbed around 500,000 tonnes less than last year at 1.1 million tonnes.
Still, the Nov-May intervention season may bring some surprises over the next two weeks when unmarketable material may be taken out of the market and offered to public stores.

Spanish grains prices fell slightly on Friday due to the beginning of the harvest season in Andalusia, traders said. They added that at first the crop seems to be lower than one year ago, but of better quality.
Especially for durum wheat.
But they added IT was too early to make a significant estimate. Barley, for which harvest season is not yet arrived, is seeing increased prices.
But traders added they were confident of a fall as soon as next week, on expectations of a good harvest and maize prices were limp because of strong imports.
Italian good mercantile soft wheat prices fell slightly over the past week due to high supply, while regular mercantile soft wheat was not traded in Turin because of a lack of the actual product.
Maize prices rose over the past week as demand started to pick up.
